newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia, Australia take stock of economic ties.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia, Australia take stock of economic ties.

text.p: Indonesian and Australian ministers met on Thursday to assess their economic ties and survey international and regional developments, Australian Foreign Minister Alexander Downer said.
Downer, leader of the six-member Australian ministerial delegation, told a news conference the meeting would focus on the two countries' economic relations.
Diplomatic sources said touchy political and diplomatic issues such as Australian concern over human rights and the East Timor issue were not expected to come up at the two-day forum.
Downer said he had discussed regional and international issues with Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas over lunch but he did not elaborate.

"This is an opportunity for Australia and Indonesia to take stock of the economic relationship and also to survey international and regional developments both of a political and economic kind," Downer said before the opening session.

"The large number of Australian ministers attending and the types of issues we will be discussing illustrate the point that the relationship that we have with Indonesia is now a very broad but also a very deep relationship," he said.
The six ministers, covering the portfolios of trade, foreign affairs, industry, transport, health and environment are in Jakarta for a two-day forum.
Downer said the Jakarta meeting was the third since the forum was set up four years ago by the previous Labor government.
The ministers will either sign or witness the signing of seven memoranda of understanding or cooperation agreements.

Trade Minister Tim Fischer, who is also Australia's deputy prime minister, said the forum would "add a great deal of cement to the bilateral relationship between Australia and Indonesia", as well as sort out thornier areas such as market access and anti-dumping procedures.

"It is a logical follow-through of the successful prime ministerial visit last month. It is putting into action our rhetoric which is to make Asia our top trade and foreign affairs policy priority," Fischer said.

While trade has been steadily growing in recent years, Australia-Indonesia political ties have often been tense, culminating with a diplomatic dispute in 1995-96 when each country rejected ambassadors nominated by the other.
Indonesia has been angered by vocal Australia-based human rights groups and their criticisms of Jakarta's policies, particularly towards the former Portuguese colony of East Timor.

East Timor resistance leader Jose Ramos Horta, who was jointly awarded the 1996 Nobel Peace Prize with East Timorese Bishop Carlos Belo, lives in self-exile in Sydney conducting an international campaign against the Jakarta government.
Indonesian troops took over the former Portuguese colony in December 1975 and the territory was declared an Indonesian province the following July.
At the last forum held in Canberra, Jakarta asked Australia to control the anti-Indonesia groups which it said were harassing Indonesian diplomats based in Australia.
